topic: reviving a mower engine after three seasons: spark, varnished jets, tank vent and valve clearances

provenance.author: CC (batch EN-1)
provenance.notes: napisane niezaleznie od korpusu PL, nie jest tlumaczeniem

base: My rotary mower has stood in the shed for three seasons and now refuses to start.
The older strimmer beside it started on the third pull despite sitting just as long.
I clipped a digital tachometer to the lead, because it counts every firing for me.
The mower gives one weak cough on cold mornings and then nothing at all afterwards.
Should I strip the carburettor first, or check for a spark before touching anything else?
Check for a spark first, because it takes two minutes and rules out half the causes.
Pull the plug, earth it against the head and watch the gap in dim light.
A weak cough often means fuel is reaching the cylinder but burning at the wrong moment.
Old petrol also loses its lighter fractions, so it will not fire in cold air.
The spark is fat and blue, so the ignition side appears to be perfectly healthy.
The petrol in the tank smells sour and has left a varnish ring around the filler.
The older strimmer ran on fresh fuel from a sealed can, which now seems important.
Is draining the tank enough, or will the varnish have reached the jets by now?
The varnish will have reached the jets, since fuel sits in the bowl for months.
Drain everything, then take the bowl off and look at the main jet against daylight.
A clear round hole should be visible, not a ragged shape or a brown film.
Clean it with solvent and a soft bristle, never with wire of any kind.
The main jet was half blocked with brown film and cleared nicely with a solvent.
The engine fires now and runs for perhaps twenty seconds before dying quite suddenly.
It will restart immediately afterwards, then die again in about the same short time.
The older strimmer still starts on the third pull without any trouble at all.
The tachometer logged the speed falling away smoothly rather than cutting out at once.
Does that point back to the carburettor, or to something in the fuel line?
That pattern points to the tank vent rather than to anything inside the carburettor.
A blocked vent lets the tank draw a vacuum until fuel can no longer flow.
Loosening the cap for a moment will confirm it, because the engine picks up instantly.
Clean the small hole in the cap with a bristle and blow it through afterwards.
Loosening the cap kept the engine running, exactly as you said that it would.
I cleared the vent hole and the mower has now run for a full half hour.
It sounds slightly harsh at the top of its range, with a faint tapping underneath.
Is that tapping worth chasing, or is it normal for an engine of this age?
A faint tapping usually means the valve clearances have opened up with wear over time.
Take the rocker cover off and measure both gaps with the piston at top centre.
Most small engines want something near four hundredths of a millimetre on the inlet side.
Adjust them cold, since a warm engine gives readings you cannot repeat next time.
Both clearances were nearly double the figure you gave and I reset them cold.
The tapping has gone and the mower pulls through thick grass without dropping its speed.
I would like to keep both machines usable through the winter without this trouble again.
Should I drain the fuel each autumn, or leave the tanks full to the top?
Drain both tanks and run each engine dry before putting them away for winter.
Fuel left standing separates and gums up exactly the passages you have just cleaned.
Pull the starter a few times with the plug out to spread oil around.
Buy petrol in small cans so that none of it stands longer than a month.
